zh.question: 天空里出现一条亮亮的流星，是远处的恒星掉下来了吗？每条亮迹都会留下陨石吗？
zh.observe: 先点“看发光的一段”，把进度往前拖一点，观察亮头前进、余迹留在原处。再点“亮光消失以后”，保持进度切换两种旅程，比较空中消散与残块继续下落。

academic.title: 三个名称指向不同对象或阶段
academic.body: 流星体是在太空中运动的小固体天体，常来自小行星或彗星碎片；流星是高速进入大气时产生的发光现象，陨石则是最终到达地面的剩余固体。它们不能与远方的恒星混为一谈。流星雨常与地球穿过碎屑流有关，而不是许多恒星一起落下；看到亮迹也不保证有可收集的陨石。

academic.title: 发光、烧蚀与破碎同时发生
academic.body: 高速入射使流星体与空气强烈相互作用，受激发气体与脱落物质参与发光，同时发生熔化、汽化和可能的破碎。向前运动的亮头与留在后方空气中的余迹不同；余迹可扩散并受风扰动。有些流星留下较长久的自发光余迹，大气化学反应也能维持发光，不能把它当成始终跟随石头的火尾。亮度还受速度、质量、成分和大气环境影响，不只由大小决定。

academic.title: 亮迹结束后可能还有暗飞行
academic.body: 有些较强残块在高速发光阶段后仍然存在。减速使强烈发光停止后，它们可继续受重力和空气阻力作用下落，称为暗飞行；高空风也会改变落点。是否留下陨石取决于入射速度、角度、强度、形状与质量，不能仅用“大石块一定落地、小石块一定消失”作判断。页面两条路线只代表两种可能结局。

zh.misconception: 流星不是恒星从天上掉下来；发光停止也不一定表示物质全都不见了。陨石是留下并到达地面的固体。
zh.boundary: 轨迹、减速、物质损失与余迹扩散采用预设教学曲线，未求解气动力、烧蚀或化学反应。尺寸、高度与各阶段时长均不按比例；选用有可见余迹的例子不表示每颗流星都有持久余迹，两种结局也不是按尺寸预测幸存或落点的判据。

narration.label: 一条亮线是什么
narration.text: 夜空里有时会闪过一条亮线，我们叫它流星。听起来像星星在跑，可是远处的恒星并没有掉下来。真正来到地球附近的，常常是一小块太空碎片。它还在太空里时，我们叫它流星体。先跟着画面里的这块小碎片走。

narration.label: 进入空气以后
narration.text: 小碎片很快地冲进地球的大气，和空气强烈相遇，就可能出现亮光，还会失去身上的物质。现在先暂停，找找它从哪里开始变亮。再往前一点：亮点走了，后面的余迹还留在刚才经过的空气里，慢慢散开。它不是一串跟着石头跑的小星星。
narration.cue: 点击“看发光的一段”，停顿约四秒；再缓慢拖动进度，比较亮头与留在后方的余迹。

narration.label: 不是每次都有落地礼物
narration.text: 有些碎片在途中就已经消散，没有石头落到地面。另一些会剩下一块，减慢速度，先不再明显发光，却还在继续往下走。把两种例子都看一遍，留意亮光消失的那一刻：碎片是真的没有了，还是只是变得不亮了？
narration.cue: 点击“亮光消失以后”，在相同进度切换两种旅程，对照消散与暗飞行。

narration.label: 三个名字串成旅程
narration.text: 如果最后真的有一块固体到达地面，它就叫陨石。我们把名字串起来：太空里的流星体，空气中的流星亮迹，可能留下的陨石。不是每段旅程都能走到最后。看到划过天空的亮光时，你已经知道，可以问它在哪里、在发生什么，而不用担心星星掉下来了。
narration.cue: 到达终点，对照三种名称。

en.question: Is a meteor a distant star falling down, and does every bright streak leave a meteorite?
en.observe: Choose “See the glowing stage” and move progress a little farther: the head advances while the wake stays behind. Choose “After the glow”, then switch journeys at the same progress to compare disappearance with a surviving piece that continues falling.

academic.title: Three names distinguish objects and phenomena
academic.body: A meteoroid is a small solid body in space, often debris from an asteroid or comet. A meteor is the luminous atmospheric phenomenon, while a meteorite is solid material that reaches the ground. None is a distant star falling. Meteor showers commonly occur when Earth meets a debris stream, and a visible streak does not guarantee recoverable meteorites.

academic.title: Light, ablation, and fragmentation
academic.body: Fast entry produces strong interaction with air. Excited gas and removed material emit light, while melting, vaporization and sometimes fragmentation remove mass. The moving luminous head differs from the wake left in the air behind it, which can disperse and respond to winds. Some meteors leave longer-lasting self-emitting trains, with atmospheric chemistry helping sustain emission. A train is not a fiery tail permanently attached to a rock. Brightness depends on speed, mass, composition and atmosphere, not size alone.

academic.title: Dark flight may continue after the glow
academic.body: Some strong fragments survive the luminous high-speed stage. After deceleration ends intense emission, they can continue falling under gravity and aerodynamic drag: dark flight. Winds also influence their landing locations. Survival depends on speed, angle, strength, shape, and mass, not simply large versus small. The two page examples illustrate possible endings, not a universal size rule.

en.misconception: A meteor is not a star falling. Losing its glow does not necessarily mean all material has vanished. A meteorite is surviving solid material that reaches the ground.
en.boundary: Path, slowing, material loss and wake spreading use prescribed teaching curves, without solving aerodynamics, ablation or chemistry. Sizes, altitudes and stage durations are not to scale. The visible-wake examples do not imply every meteor has a persistent train, and the two endings do not predict survival or landing location from size.

narration.label: What makes that bright line?
narration.text: Sometimes a bright line flashes across the night sky. We call it a meteor, or a shooting star, but a distant star has not fallen. The traveler is often a small piece of space debris. While it is still in space, it is called a meteoroid. Let’s follow the little fragment in our picture.
narration.cue: Advance slowly from the space starting point.

narration.label: Meeting the air
narration.text: The fragment rushes into Earth’s atmosphere and meets the air very strongly. It can glow while losing some of its material. Pause and find where the light begins. Now move a little farther. The bright head has moved on, but the wake stays in the air it just passed through and slowly spreads. It is not a string of little stars following the rock.
narration.cue: Choose “See the glowing stage”, pause for four seconds, then slowly advance progress to compare the head with its wake.

narration.label: Not every trip reaches the ground
narration.text: Some fragments disappear along the way and leave no rock on the ground. Others leave a piece that slows down, stops glowing brightly, and keeps falling. Try both examples. When the light disappears, has the fragment really gone, or has it simply stopped shining? Look carefully for the remaining piece.
narration.cue: Choose “After the glow” and switch journeys at the same progress to compare disappearance with dark flight.

narration.label: Three names for the journey
narration.text: If a solid piece reaches the ground, it is called a meteorite. Put the names together: a meteoroid in space, a meteor’s bright atmospheric streak, and perhaps a meteorite left at the end. Not every journey reaches that final stage. Now a flashing line in the sky can make you wonder what is happening, without thinking a star has fallen.
narration.cue: Finish at the endpoint and compare the three terms.
